documents.title: Economic burden of five common cancers in Iran: a systematic review of cost-of-illness with a focus on healthcare resource utilization.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: According to the latest World Health Organization report, approximately half of the new cancer cases in Iran are attributed to five common cancers: gastric, breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer. These cancers impose a heavy economic burden on healthcare systems and society, including direct medical costs (DMC), direct non-medical costs (DNMC), and indirect costs (IDC). This systematic review aimed to investigate the economic burden of these cancers in Iran.
METHODS: This systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. The search strategy was developed using MeSH terms, Emtree, and previous literature. To identify relevant studies published up until December 27, 2023, searches were conducted in both international databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane, and the NHS Economic Evaluation Database) and national databases (SID, Magiran, and IranMedex). After removing duplicates and screening studies using Endnote software, eligible studies were selected for inclusion in the review. The costs were converted to USD 2021 using the CCEMG-EPPI-Centre cost converter.
RESULTS: A total of 22 studies were included in this review. Breast and colorectal cancer each had 4 studies, while prostate, gastric, and lung cancer each had 3 studies. The remaining 5 studies covered a combination of multiple cancers. Converting the costs from different studies to USD 2021 showed that the average annual DMC per patient with breast cancer varied from $13,954 to $34,772. These costs ranged from $14,671 to $28,656 for colorectal cancer, $7,970 to $16,821 for prostate cancer, $12,206 to $17,681 for gastric cancer, and $9,369 to $40,682 for lung cancer. Part of these variations may be related to differences in healthcare resource utilization, while another part may be due to differences in cost calculation methodology, study perspective, and study location. Additional cost conversion findings showed that in 85% of the studies, the average annual DNMC per patient for all cancers were estimated to be less than $4,000. Furthermore, the average annual IDC per patient for breast and lung cancer were estimated to be as high as $100,000 due to high mortality, compared to less than $30,000 for other cancers.
CONCLUSIONS: Given the high prevalence of these five cancers in Iran, their economic burden is significant. Policymakers should focus not only on reducing the disease burden but also on minimizing the economic burden of cancer. Strategies such as improving early detection, optimizing treatment pathways, and implementing cost-effective interventions could help reduce both healthcare costs and the overall financial strain on patients and the healthcare system.

These costs ranged from $14,671 to $28,656 for colorectal cancer, $7,970 to $16,821 for prostate cancer, $12,206 to $17,681 for gastric cancer, and $9,369 to $40,682 for lung cancer. Part of these variations may be related to differences in healthcare resource utilization, while another part may be due to differences in cost calculation methodology, study perspective, and study location. Additional cost conversion findings showed that in 85% of the studies, the average annual DNMC per patient for all cancers were estimated to be less than $4,000. Furthermore, the average annual IDC per patient for breast and lung cancer were estimated to be as high as $100,000 due to high mortality, compared to less than $30,000 for other cancers. Conclusions Given the high prevalence of these five cancers in Iran, their economic burden is significant. Policymakers should focus not only on reducing the disease burden but also on minimizing the economic burden of cancer. Strategies such as improving early detection, optimizing treatment pathways, and implementing cost-effective interventions could help reduce both healthcare costs and the overall financial strain on patients and the healthcare system. Background Iran, as a middle-income and developing country, has experienced a growing burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) in recent decades due to demographic and epidemiological transitions, including an aging population and the increase in risk factors such as smoking, poor diet, and physical inactivity [ 1 ]. Among NCDs, cancer is the second leading cause of death and represents a significant portion of the disease burden, imposing a heavy strain on the healthcare system and Iranian society [ 2 ]. According to the latest GLOBOCAN report (published in 2024) on cancer incidence and mortality for the year 2022, more than 137,000 new cancer cases and approximately 87,000 cancer-related deaths occurred in Iran. The report highlights that nearly half of these new cases are attributed to five cancers—stomach (gastric), breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate—which account for the highest incidence rates in the general population (both sexes) [ 3 ]. Furthermore, projections indicate that, after thyroid cancer, prostate, breast, and colorectal cancers will experience the largest increases in new cases by 2025. The total number of new cancer cases is projected to increase by 42.6% compared to 2016, reaching an estimated 160,000 new cases in 2025 [ 4 ]. Additionally, the latest statistics from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021(GBD 2021) highlight that gastric, lung, and breast cancers have the highest disease burden in Iran (measured by Disability-Adjusted Life Years, DALYs), and also, colorectal and prostate cancers rank sixth and eighth, respectively [ 5 ]. Cancer not only affects public health but also significantly impacts the country’s economy [ 6 ]. The increasing economic burden of cancer is a growing concern, particularly as healthcare resources become strained and the demand for cancer treatment rises. Given the high prevalence of these five cancers in Iran, the cost of illness for these cancers is substantial. Cost of illness studies generally classify costs into three categories: direct costs (including direct medical costs (DMC) and direct non-medical costs (DNMC)), indirect costs (IDC), and intangible costs. Since intangible costs are rarely quantified in cost of illness studies due to measurement challenges and related debates, the focus is mainly on the first two categories. DMC refers to the costs of healthcare resource utilization for diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, etc., while DNMC covers non-healthcare resources such as transportation and accommodation. IDC reflects productivity losses due to morbidity and mortality incurred by patients. All these costs contribute to the overall economic burden of disease [ 7 , 8 ]. Therefore, quantification and investigation of these costs for common cancers are necessary to better understand the full impact of the disease. By examining these costs for five cancers, it is possible to determine which factors have the greatest impact on costs and help health managers implement policies with appropriate prioritization. This information can assist policymakers and health planners in making better decisions regarding resource allocation and prioritization. Additionally, examining costs can play an important role in raising awareness among policymakers and health planners about the economic and social burden of cancer. Increased awareness of the financial and economic effects of cancer can help shape positive attitudes and greater attention toward the prevention and management of this disease. Therefore, considering the importance of the issue, this systematic review aimed to investigate the economic burden of five common cancers in Iran: breast, gastric, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer. The qualitative findings of this review can assist researchers in designing future studies on the economic burden of cancer, while the quantitative findings provide valuable data for policymakers to help prevent and reduce the disease burden. Methods This systematic review focuses on five common cancers in Iran: gastric, breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer. These cancer types were selected due to their highest incidence and one-year prevalence rates for the general population (both sexes), as reported in the latest GLOBOCAN 2022 data. The selection reflects the significant public health impact and economic burden these cancers pose to the Iranian society. Detailed incidence and prevalence rates are provided in the Supplementary Material 1 . This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 9 ]. The completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided in the Supplementary Material 2 . Review question What is the economic burden of five common cancers in Iran? Eligibility criteria All the studies that investigated the cost of illness or the economic burden of five common cancers in Iran were reviewed without considering the time limit. The exclusion criteria for the review include the following: (1) Types of studies such as editorials, letters to the editor, systematic and non-systematic review, meta-analysis, case reports, clinical trials, and conference summaries. (2) Studies that estimated case-specific components of cancer costs (e.g., only surgery or drugs, etc.). (3) Studies that have dealt with only specific analyses such as cost-effectiveness, cost-utility, cost-benefit, and cost minimization. Determining data sources Scientific sources included original studies available in international databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane, and the NHS Economic Evaluation Database. In this review, manual searches in Google and Google Scholar were also used to complete the review and make it comprehensive. In addition, gray literature was reviewed using a modified search strategy from the OpenGrey database. The Scientific Information Database (SID), Magiran, and IranMedex national databases were also used to search for studies published in Persian. The search was conducted in these databases without any time limitations, covering all studies published up until December 27, 2023. Search strategy design The search strategy was designed using PEO components. In this review, the population (P) considered for the search of published studies included any individual or groups of Iranian nationality, regardless of age, gender, race, or socioeconomic status, who were exposed (E) to the five common cancers. The outcome (O) sought information on healthcare resource utilization and the economic burden associated with exposure to these five cancers. The keywords related to these components were identified from Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, Emtree, and previous literature. To consider language and terminology differences, national databases (SID, Magiran, and IranMedex) were searched using equivalent Persian terms for selected keywords. After identifying the appropriate keywords, search strategies were developed for each database by balancing sensitivity and accuracy indicators. The developed strategy for searching in four international databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase) is provided in Supplementary Material 3 . Selection of relevant studies At this step of the review, studies were extracted from selected databases according to the developed search strategy. Duplicates were then removed using Endnote V.20.2.1 software. The remaining studies underwent screening based on the eligibility criteria in two phases. The first phase involved screening based on the title and abstract, while the second phase involved screening based on the full text. The screening process was performed by two reviewers (KI and JA) independently, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus with a third reviewer (VA). The screening of studies followed PRISMA principles. Data collection and extraction A tool was created using Excel 2016 software to collect data required for the variables of this review from the studies. The tool included three tables: one for the characteristics of the included studies, one for cost components of the included studies and one for cost findings of the included studies. The table of study characteristics included variables such as the study’s target population, perspective, time frame, sample size, sampling method, currency, costing year, discount rate, and study design method. The table of cost components included the cost items, their data sources, and their cost calculation methods for three cost groups: direct medical costs (DMC), direct non-medical costs (DNMC), and indirect costs (IDC). The table of cost findings included the cost results and cost synthesis for these three cost groups. Data synthesis In this review, cost findings were converted to 2021 United States dollar (USD) using the Campbell and Cochrane Economics Methods Group Evidence for Policy and Practice Information and Coordination Centre (CCEMG-EPPI-Centre) cost converter (v.1.7, last updated: January 2024). In this converter, we used the International Monetary Fund (IMF) method, which adjusts costs based on purchasing power parity (PPP) values. The IMF method first adjusts costs using the Gross Domestic Product Deflator index, which accounts for inflation and economic conditions in each country. Then, the adjusted costs are converted to USD using PPP exchange rates, which account for differences in purchasing power between countries [ 10 ]. The year 2021 was selected for conversion because among the studies included in this review, the most recent year of cost calculation was 2021. Quality assessment of studies In this review, quality assessment was performed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ 11 ]. This scale has recently been applied to assess quality in several reviews on the economic burden of cancer [ 12 – 14 ]. The NOS is a multi-star system, originally designed for cohort and case-control studies, but modified versions are available for evaluating the quality of cross-sectional studies. The modified NOS assesses the methodological rigor of cross-sectional studies, similarly to cohort studies, across three domains: selection, comparability, and outcome, which are also applicable to retrospective studies. The population selection domain evaluated sample representativeness (4 or 5 stars), the population comparability domain evaluated the comparability of subjects (2 stars), and the outcome domain evaluated statistical testing and outcome assessment (3 stars) [ 12 ]. A quality score for each study was calculated by summing the awarded stars. Thus, studies with ≥ 8 stars were categorized as high-quality, 5–7 stars as moderate quality, and ≤ 4 stars as low quality [ 15 ]. Results Overview A total of 6,179 studies were retrieved by searching the developed search strategy in the databases. After removing duplicate studies using Endnote V.20.2.1 software, 4,593 studies entered the screening phase. During the first phase of screening, studies were reviewed based on the title and abstract. In this phase, 4,533 studies were excluded due to irrelevance, leaving 60 studies for the second phase of screening. In the second phase, the full text of the remaining studies was examined, resulting in the exclusion of 37 studies due to a lack of eligibility criteria. Among these, 2 studies were excluded despite meeting the criteria due to incorrect outcomes [ 16 , 17 ]. Finally, a quality assessment was conducted for the remaining 23 studies. One article was excluded due to low quality [ 18 ]. Among the assessed studies, 22 received acceptable grades (6 with good quality and 16 with moderate quality) and remained for the final review (Fig. 1 ). The quality assessment results are provided in the Supplementary Material 4 . Fig. 1 PRISMA diagram of the search and selection process Characteristics of included studies Among the 22 studies included in this review, 4 studies related to breast cancer [ 19 – 22 ], 4 studies related to colorectal cancer [ 23 – 26 ], 3 studies related to prostate cancer [ 27 – 29 ], 3 studies related to gastric cancer [ 30 – 32 ], 3 studies related to lung cancer [ 33 – 35 ], and 5 studies related to a combination of multiple cancers [ 36 – 40 ]. Most of these studies examined costs from a societal perspective ( N = 7) and patient’s perspective ( N = 7). The time period for most studies was 1 year ( N = 9). Among the studies that mentioned the sampling method in their report, the census method ( N = 6) followed by the random sampling method ( N = 4) had the largest number. The sample size in most studies was below 200 people ( N = 8). In most studies, the costs were reported in USD ( N = 18). The study design method in most studies was cross-sectional ( N = 14) (Table 1 , Fig. 2 ). Fig. 3 Average annual DMC, DNMC, and IDC per cancer patient in Iran In Jalali et al.’s study, the average DNMC per breast cancer patient in 2021 were $2,087. These costs include accommodation, transportation for patients and companions, food for patients and companions, telephone and internet contact with family, shopping for assistive devices, babysitting, and housemaids [ 19 ]. In the study by Afkar et al., the costs for the private and public sectors in 2017 were estimated at $170 and $340, respectively, taking into account the costs of accommodation, transportation, and food [ 20 ]. In Daroudi et al.’s study in 2011, these costs were approximately $550, considering transportation costs [ 21 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per breast cancer patient in these studies varied from $1,156 to $3,439 (mean = $2,481; median = $2,849) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per breast cancer patient in the study by Jalali et al. in 2021 were $1,425 [ 19 ]. In Afkar et al.’s study in 2017, these costs were estimated at $1,870 for the private sector and $22,350 for the public sector [ 20 ]. In Daroudi et al.’s study in 2011, these costs were approximately $19,000 [ 21 ]. In Jalali et al.’s study, these costs only considered the lost productivity due to the absence of patients and their companions. However, Afkar et al.’s study and Daroudi et al.’s study included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their family, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per breast cancer patient in these three studies were $2,348, $50,426, and $98,891, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Colorectal cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for colorectal cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, inpatient hospital care (such as the costs of inpatient drugs, nursing care, and use of inpatient resources), diagnostic services, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, rehabilitation such as physiotherapy, as well as medication and drugs. The costs of diagnostic services include laboratory tests, pathology, computed tomography scan (CT scan), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasonography, electrocardiography, electroencephalography, radiography, nuclear medicine, endoscopy, and other diagnostic laboratory and radiology services [ 23 – 26 ] (Table 2 ). In Jafari et al.’s study, the average DMC per colorectal cancer patient in 2019 were estimated to be $4,301 (1 USD = 42,000 IRR) [ 23 ]. In Nejati et al.’s study, these costs for 2016 were equivalent to $17,038 (1 USD = 8,212.15 IRR) [ 24 ], and in Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study for 2012 and in Davari et al.’s study for 2011, the costs were equivalent to $4,242 (1 USD = 12,229 IRR) and $7,768 (1 USD = 10,965 IRR), respectively [ 25 , 26 ]. Additionally, Jafari et al. estimated the total costs for colorectal cancer in 2019 to be $46 million for the whole country. In the study by Vahdatimanesh et al. in 2012, these total costs were estimated at $96 million (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with colorectal cancer in different studies varied from $14,671 to $28,656 (mean = $20,840; median = $20,016) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per colorectal cancer patient in Jafari et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of accommodation, transportation of patients and companions, food for the patient and companions, special diet, changing the home environment to adapt to the disease, telephone and internet calls to family, babysitters and kindergartens, and purchase of aids, were estimated at $949 in 2019 [ 23 ]. These costs were estimated to be $4,388 in 2016 in the study by Nejati et al., who included the costs of guardian services and hoteling as DNMC [ 24 ]. In Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study in 2012, the costs were approximately $1,297, considering the costs of patient time and transportation as DNMC [ 25 ]. Jafari et al. estimated these costs for the whole country to be $10 million, while Vahdatimanesh et al. estimated them at $29 million (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per colorectal cancer patient in these studies varied from $3,526 to $6,193 (mean = $4,735; median= $4,485) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per colorectal cancer patient in the study by Jafari et al. in 2019 were estimated to be $495 [ 23 ]. In Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study, these costs were estimated to be approximately $7,659 per patient and $173 million for the whole country in 2012 [ 25 ]. In Jafari et al.’s study, these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, whereas in Vahdatimanesh et al.’s study, these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per colorectal cancer patient in these two studies were $1,841 and $26,490, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Prostate cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for prostate cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services (such as imaging and cystoscopy, laboratory and pathology services), surgery (including radical prostatectomy and orchiectomy surgery), radiotherapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, rehabilitation, as well as medication and drugs (such as antiandrogens and luteinizing hormone agonists) [ 27 – 29 ] (Table 2 ). In Alinezhad et al.’s study, the average DMC per prostate cancer patient in 2018 were estimated to be $3,773 PPP (exchange rate not reported) [ 27 ]. In Foroughi Moghadam et al.’s study, these costs for 2015 were equivalent to $2,934 (1 USD = 29,580 IRR) [ 28 ]. Mojahidian et al.’s study in 2016 reported these costs by different disease states, ranging from $103 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $7,748 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer (exchange rate not reported) [ 29 ]. The DMC of prostate cancer for the whole country were estimated at $2 million in Alinezhad et al.’s study and $12.5 million in Foroughi Moghadam et al.’s study (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with prostate cancer in different studies varied from $7,970 to $16,821 (mean = $13,704; median = $16,320) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per prostate cancer patient in Alinezhad et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of transportation, accommodation, and a disease-specific diet in 2018, were estimated to be $186 PPP [ 27 ]. In the study by Mojahidian et al., these costs, considering the costs of intra-city and inter-city travel to receive services, hotel accommodation, and food consumed during the trip in 2016, varied from $97 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $1,068 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer [ 29 ]. In the study by Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs were estimated to be approximately $200 per patient and $898 thousand for the whole country based on the new cases identified in 2015, considering the costs of transportation and accommodation as DNMC [ 28 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per prostate cancer patient in these studies varied from $300 to $2,652 (mean = $1,374; median = $1,171) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per prostate cancer patient in the study by Alinezhad et al. in 2018 were estimated to be $1,307 PPP [ 27 ]. These costs varied based on different disease states and were reported in the study by Mojahidian et al. in 2016, ranging from $24 for low-risk metastatic prostate cancer to $358 for resistant metastatic prostate cancer [ 29 ]. In the study by Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs were estimated to be approximately $2,920 per patient and $12 million for the whole country, based on the new cases identified in 2015 [ 28 ]. Alinezhad et al. included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death. However, in the studies by Mojahidian et al. and Foroughi Moghadam et al., these costs only included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and the patient’s family (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per prostate cancer patient in these three studies were $10,857, $739, and $16,239, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Gastric cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for gastric cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services (such as initial tests, pre-chemotherapy tests, follow-up tests, CT scan, MRI, ultrasonography, endoscopy, colonoscopy, and other diagnostic laboratory and radiology services), surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, as well as medication and drugs (including the costs of chemotherapy drugs, supportive drugs) [ 30 – 32 ] (Table 2 ). In the study by Jalilian et al., the average DMC per gastric cancer patient in 2017 were estimated to be $3,288 (1 USD = 32,441 IRR) [ 30 ]. In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs for 2016 were equivalent to $2,350 (1 USD = 30,221 IRR) [ 31 ]. In the study by Izadi et al., these costs in 2015 were estimated to be 113,370,129 Rials for the private sector and 74,705,158 Rials for the public sector [ 32 ] (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with gastric cancer in different studies varied from $12,206 to $17,681 (mean = $15,369; median = $16,220) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average DNMC per gastric cancer patient in Jalilian et al.’s study, taking into account the costs of travel, accommodation, and food in 2017, were estimated to be $378 [ 30 ]. In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs were equal to $522 for 2016, considering the costs of transportation, accommodation, food for the patient and relatives, the patient’s consumables, and the accommodation of the people who visit the patient at his, her home [ 31 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per gastric cancer patient in these studies varied from $1,862 to $2,711 (mean = median = $2,287) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per gastric cancer patient in the study by Jalilian et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $505 [ 30 ]. I In the study by Eghdami et al., these costs for 2016 were equal to $1,094 [ 31 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and the patient’s companions (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per gastric cancer patient in these two studies were $2,493 and $5,682, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Lung cancer The findings of this review show that DMC for lung cancer encompass various healthcare resource utilization or cost items, including specialist visits, hospitalization, diagnostic services, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, physiotherapy, as well as medication and drugs [ 33 – 35 ] (Table 2 ). In Mir et al.’s study, the average DMC per lung cancer patient in 2016 were estimated to be $7,542 (exchange rate not reported) [ 33 ]. In Mohagheghi et al.’s study, these costs for 2009 were equivalent to $1,932 (1 USD = 9,917 IRR) [ 35 ]. Additionally, Mohagheghi et al. estimated the total costs for lung cancer in 2009 to be $11 million for the whole country based on the incidence of the disease. In Rezaei et al.’s study, these total costs were estimated to be 350 billion Rials for the whole country based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ] (Table 3 ). Converting the costs to USD 2021 showed that the average DMC per patient with lung cancer in different studies varied from $9,369 to $40,682 (mean = $21,280; median = $13,785) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). In the study by Mir et al., the average DNMC per lung cancer patient in 2016, taking into account the costs of transportation, food, and accommodation, were estimated to be $499 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs, considering transportation, accommodation, food, care for family members such as the elderly or children, and other service costs such as telephone bills for the whole country based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014, were estimated at 87 billion Rials [ 34 ] (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average DNMC per lung cancer patient in these studies varied from $2,690 to $3,428 (mean = median = $3,059) (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per lung cancer patient in the study by Mir et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $11,903 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs for the whole country were estimated to be approximately 584 million Rials per patient and 2,789 billion Rials based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per lung cancer patient in these two studies were $64,207 and $110,015, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). The average IDC per lung cancer patient in the study by Mir et al. in 2017 were estimated to be $11,903 [ 33 ]. In the study by Rezaei et al., these costs for the whole country were estimated to be approximately 584 million Rials per patient and 2,789 billion Rials based on the 5-year prevalence of the disease in 2014 [ 34 ]. Both studies included the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient and their companions, as well as the costs of lost productivity due to premature death (Table 3 ). Based on USD 2021, the average IDC per lung cancer patient in these two studies were $64,207 and $110,015, respectively (Table 3 , Fig. 3 ). Discussion As the findings indicate, the healthcare resource utilization or cost items for DMC may vary depending on the type of cancer, while the cost items for DNMC and IDC are similar for all cancers. Most of the differences among cost items for DMC are linked to diagnostic services. For instance, one of the cost items for breast cancer that other cancers do not have is the diagnostic cost of mammography. Similarly, one of the cost items for colorectal cancer that other cancers do not have is the diagnostic cost of colonoscopy. This highlights the importance of recognizing the unique cost drivers for each cancer type in healthcare planning, as they contribute significantly to the overall economic burden. Converting the costs from different studies to USD 2021 showed that the average annual DMC per patient with breast cancer in Iran varied from $13,954 to $34,772 [ 19 – 22 ]. These costs range from $14,671 to $28,656 for colorectal cancer [ 23 – 26 ], $7,970 to $16,821 for prostate cancer [ 27 – 29 ], $12,206 to $17,681 for gastric cancer [ 30 – 32 ], and $9,369 to $40,682 for lung cancer [ 33 – 35 ]. Part of this variation is related to the different healthcare resource utilization or cost items considered for cost calculation. Another part may be due to differences in cost calculation methodology, study perspective, and study location (private or public sector). The observed cost variation reflects the complex interplay of healthcare policies, resource availability, and methodological choices across different studies. Since these five cancers are the most common cancers in Iran, multiplying these costs by the total number of people with cancer makes the total cost for the country significant. For example, in the study by Daroudi et al. in 2010, the costs for breast cancer in the whole country were estimated at $176 million [ 21 ]. Therefore, the researchers emphasize that the disease burden is one dimension of the problem, and the other dimension is the economic burden of the disease, which, if not addressed, can have significant effects on the country’s health economics. Without targeted policies to reduce diagnostic and treatment costs, this economic pressure may challenge the sustainability of Iran’s healthcare system. The cost items for DNMC are similar across all cancers. These items include the costs of accommodation, transportation for patients and companions (both intra-city and inter-city), food for patients and companions, special diets, telephone and internet communication with family, purchasing auxiliary equipment, patient consumables, modifying the home environment to adapt to the disease, childcare, eldercare, kindergarten services, hiring a housemaid, and accommodating visitors at the patient’s home [ 19 – 21 , 23 – 25 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. However, due to limitations in measuring these costs, some cost items might be ignored or simpler methods might be used to measure them. Ignoring certain DNMC items may lead to an underestimation of the total economic burden, especially in cases where these costs are substantial, potentially resulting in insufficient resource allocation and inadequate support for patients and their families. Based on USD 2021, in 85% of studies (11 out of 13 studies), the average annual DNMC per patient are estimated to be less than $4,000 for each patient suffering from one of these five cancers [ 19 – 21 , 23 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. In other studies, (2 out of 13 studies), these costs were more than $4,000 that were related to colorectal cancer [ 24 , 25 ]. This finding suggests that DNMC, though generally lower than DMC, still represent a significant burden, particularly for cancers like colorectal cancer where these costs exceed $4,000, underscoring the need for comprehensive support systems for cancer patients and their families. The authors believe that the similarity in DNMC across cancers reflects broader socioeconomic impacts on patients and their families, highlighting the need for universal support services that address non-medical costs among cancer patients. IDC, like DNMC, have similar cost items across all cancers. These items include the costs of lost productivity due to the patient’s absence from work, the costs of lost productivity due to the absence of the patient’s companions who care for them, and the costs of lost productivity due to premature death [ 19 – 21 , 23 – 25 , 27 – 31 , 33 , 34 ]. It is important to consider that due to limitations in measurement, some of these cost items may be ignored in studies, or they may be measured based on assumptions. Since the death and disability rate is much higher in some cancers compared to others, the variance of these costs may be significant among different cancers. For instance, based on USD 2021, the average annual IDC per patient with breast and lung cancer, due to high mortality, were approximately $100,000 [ 34 ], while for other cancers, the average annual IDC were less than $30,000 [ 25 , 27 ]. The researchers conclude that the high IDC associated with cancers like breast and lung cancer, driven by high mortality rates, calls for more preventive and early detection programs to reduce productivity loss. Focusing on these high-mortality cancers could further help alleviate both individual and national economic burdens. Given the complexity of measuring, future research could focus on refining cost measurement techniques, particularly for DNMC and IDC, and addressing methodological differences across studies. Additionally, exploring how integrating cancer support services, such as palliative care, psychological support, and family care, might reduce some of these non-medical and indirect costs would be valuable. Limitations Since this review is related to Iran and almost all studies from this country have been published in Persian and English, we did not face significant language limitations. However, since most of the studies focus on specific regions or healthcare settings within Iran, the findings may not be fully generalizable to all regions or healthcare environments in the country. Additionally, due to the nature of the search strategy and the selected databases, there is always the possibility of missing studies in a systematic review. To reduce this limitation, we developed a detailed search strategy and selected diverse databases. Finally, due to the heterogeneous nature of cost definitions and measurements among the included studies in this review, comparing costs across studies was difficult. Therefore, in the study findings section, efforts were made to compare costs more cautiously, and for this purpose, the findings have been reported in more detail. Conclusion Cancer encompasses a wide range of resources and cost items. For researchers to accurately examine DMC, DNMC, and IDC in future studies, they should aim to include all or at least most of these cost items in their calculations. Despite the limitations in calculating some of these costs, findings from studies indicate that the costs associated with the five most common cancers in Iran are significant. Therefore, efforts by policymakers to combat cancer should not only focus on reducing the burden of the disease but also aim to alleviate the economic burden it imposes. To achieve this, policymakers could consider implementing more efficient resource allocation strategies, enhancing access to early detection and preventive programs, and investing in cost-effective treatment protocols. Additionally, establishing financial support systems for patients, particularly for non-medical costs, could mitigate the economic challenges faced by cancer patients and their families. documents.title: Ethnic differences in prostate-specific antigen levels in men without prostate cancer: a systematic review.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Black men are twice as likely to be diagnosed with prostate cancer than White men. Raised prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels can indicate an increased risk of prostate cancer, however it is not known whether PSA levels differ for men of different ethnic groups.
METHODS: PubMed and Embase were searched to identify studies that reported levels of PSA for men of at least two ethnic groups without a prostate cancer diagnosis or symptoms suggestive of prostate cancer. An adaptation of the Newcastle-Ottawa scale was used to assess risk of bias and study quality. Findings were stratified into the following broad ethnic groups: White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, and Other. Data were analysed in a narrative synthesis due to the heterogeneity of reported PSA measures and methods in the included studies.
RESULTS: A total of 654 197 males from 13 studies were included. By ethnicity, this included 536 201 White (82%), 38 287 Black (6%), 38 232 Asian (6%), 18 029 Pacific Island (3%), 13 614 Maori (2%), 8 885 Hispanic (1%), and 949 Other (<1%) men aged ≥40 years old. Black men had higher PSA levels than White men, and Hispanic men had similar levels to White men and lower levels than Black men.
CONCLUSIONS: Black men without prostate cancer have higher PSA levels than White or Hispanic men, which reflects the higher rates of prostate cancer diagnosis in Black men. Despite that, the diagnostic accuracy of PSA for prostate cancer for men of different ethnic groups is unknown, and current guidance for PSA test interpretation does not account for ethnicity. Future research needs to determine whether Black men are diagnosed with similar rates of clinically significant prostate cancer to White men, or whether raised PSA levels are contributing to overdiagnosis of prostate cancer in Black men.

Introduction Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer death in males worldwide with 357 000 annual deaths [ 1 ]. Incidence and mortality of prostate cancer differ according to ethnicity: each are twice as high in Black males compared to White males in both the USA [ 2 , 3 ] and the UK [ 4 – 6 ], whereas Asian men in the UK experience lower rates [ 4 – 6 ]. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is a protein secreted by the prostate gland and is measured through blood testing. PSA can be elevated in patients with prostate cancer or benign prostate disease; it does not accurately discriminate between the two and the benefits of PSA screening are unclear [ 7 – 11 ]. Evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of PSA in symptomatic men is focussed on the referred population, and the performance in men consulting primary care is unknown [ 12 ]. The most recent systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of PSA for prostate cancer in patients with lower urinary tract symptoms found that a PSA threshold of 4 ng/mL had a sensitivity of 0.93 (95% CI 0.88, 0.96) specificity of 0.20 (95% CI 0.12, 0.33), and the Area Under the Curve (AUC) was 0.72 (95% CI 0.68, 0.76), although this did not factor in patient ethnicity and studies were at high risk of bias [ 13 ]. To assess a patient’s risk of prostate cancer in the USA, doctors are encouraged to use their clinical judgement of a patient’s PSA level in combination with factors that elevate their risk (such as whether a patient is of Black ethnicity). Patients are then referred for further tests or monitoring if necessary [ 14 ]. In the UK, guidance from the National Institute of Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) provides age-specific PSA thresholds to assess a patient’s risk of prostate cancer [ 15 ]. These guidelines recommend that men with a PSA above age-specific thresholds should be offered investigation and referral for suspected prostate cancer, but does not take into account the patient’s ethnicity. A recent systematic review found ethnicity to be a considerable source of heterogeneity when assessing age-adjusted PSA reference ranges and concluded ethnicity should be considered when clinically assessing PSA levels [ 16 ]. There is currently no ethnicity specific guidance for interpreting PSA results although previous studies have considered ethnicity-specific PSA thresholds [ 17 – 19 ]. Identifying differences in PSA levels in men of different ethnic groups without prostate cancer could help refine the identification of men who may benefit from investigation for suspected prostate cancer. This systematic review sought to identify studies that reported PSA levels for different ethnic groups for men without a prostate cancer diagnosis or symptoms suggestive of prostate cancer and incorporated the findings from these studies into a narrative synthesis to determine the effects of ethnicity on PSA. Methods Protocol This systematic review closely adhered to the study protocol which was published on the PROSPERO website on the 29 th September 2021 before commencement of abstract screening (reference CRD42021274580) and was conducted in strict accordance to the PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines. Eligibility criteria This review aimed to identify studies that reported measures of PSA levels of men without a prostate cancer diagnosis or symptoms suggestive of prostate cancer for at least two different ethnic groups. Studies that only included PSA values for only one ethnic group were excluded to reduce selection, design, measurement, and reporting bias. We included observational studies and randomised controlled trials with baseline characteristics, but excluded studies based on cases and matched controls. Only studies with the full text available and peer reviewed in English were included. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are available in Table 1 . Table 1 Inclusion and exclusion criteria for study inclusion eligibility. Inclusion Exclusion Adults aged ≥18 years Children / animals Recruited from a general population (populations selected due to age are acceptable provided this is consistent for each ethnic group) Recruited due to disease or symptom status (e.g. prostate cancer), medication usage, or other ‘non-general’ population (e.g. healthcare workers, pregnant women, marathon runners etc.) Available PSA test result as raw values, a pooled average (e.g. mean, median, range, centiles) or proportion above or below a certain figure No available PSA test result PSA values must be stratified by broad ethnic group No stratification of PSA level by broad ethnic group More than one ethnic group reported Only one ethnic group reported Observational studies without matching Matched observational studies Baseline PSA values from randomised controlled trials PSA levels reported after intervention in randomised controlled trials Peer reviewed, full text available in English Abstracts, full texts not peer-reviewed or available in English Search strategy PubMed and Embase were searched on the 24 th September 2021 and again on the 21 st June 2022 to identify studies that reported levels of PSA for at least two ethnic groups. Search terms included prostate-specific antigen or PSA and ethnicity or ethnic group. To capture all ethnicity or ethnic groups, the search included mESH terms for a number of ancestry groups such as African, European, Asian, American Native, and Oceanic, mESH terms for Ethnic Groups and Minority Groups, as well as commonly used terms to describe ethnic groups such as African*, Caucas*, Europ*, Asian*, Indian*, Maori*, Hispanic*, Chinese* etc. The terms White and Black were included if they appeared within three words of ethnic* in attempt to reduce non-specific search returns. Full search terms can be found in Appendix 1. Endnote X9 was used to automatically detect duplicates which was followed by manual detection by one reviewer. Two reviewers independently screened abstracts and full texts for eligibility and conflicts were resolved by discussion with a third reviewer. Cohen’s kappa was calculated to assess interrater reliability. Data extraction Data extraction was completed independently by two reviewers and cross-referenced for discrepancies. The following data were extracted: number and age of patients, country of study, the context in which PSA levels were collected (healthcare records vs PSA test in general population), ascertainment of ethnicity, and PSA measures (median, mean, centiles, proportion above/below) for each ethnic group. Given that age is a factor in PSA variation, age-stratified or age-adjusted levels were extracted where reported. Quality assessment As this systematic review extracted PSA measures from a variety of study designs, an adaptation of the Newcastle-Ottawa scale for cohort studies was used to assess the quality and risk of bias of the included studies, addressing the aims of this review rather than the individual aims of the included papers. The adaptation of the Newcastle-Ottawa assessment can be found in Appendix 2. Two reviewers independently scored each paper based on selection, comparability, and outcome domains for a maximum of nine stars. Conflicts were resolved by discussion. Each study was then classed as ‘good’, ‘fair’, or ‘poor’ based on the Newcastle-Ottawa thresholds. Data synthesis Participants were stratified into the following broad ethnic groups based on the classification used in the included papers: White (including White, Caucasian, European), Black (Black, African American, non-Hispanic Black), Asian (Asian), Hispanic (Hispanic, Latino, Mexican-American), and Other (Other, Maori, Pacific Island, Pacific People). Where studies reported more than one summary statistic for PSA values, the summary statistic most comparable with other extractions was chosen for the final table (most often median and 95 th percentile). If statistical significance was not reported, confidence intervals were calculated from the mean and standard deviation where possible to infer significance. Studies that were assessed as poor quality were considered separately to studies that were assessed as fair or good in a narrative sensitivity analysis. Due to significant heterogeneity in the reported measures of PSA, meta-analysis was not possible. Therefore, results were collated and summarised into a narrative synthesis following previously published guidance [ 20 ]. Results Database search The database search returned 441 studies, from which 166 duplicates and 243 irrelevant studies were excluded based on title and abstract. This left 32 studies for full-text review, of which 19 studies were excluded and resulted in 13 studies included in the narrative synthesis (Fig. 1 ). The level of inter-rater reliability was moderate (0.57, Cohen’s kappa) for abstract screening and substantial (0.64, Cohen’s kappa) for full-text screening. Fig. 1 Flow diagram of the study selection process. Study quality Just over half (7/13) of the included studies were assessed as high quality (good) using the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa scale, with the remainder rated as poor. Narrative synthesis Ten studies reported PSA values for White and Black men, all conducted in the USA. Half of these studies found higher PSA levels in Black men compared with White men [ 18 , 19 , 21 , 24 , 25 ], one study found the opposite [ 23 ], while the remaining four studies found no difference between men of both groups [ 17 , 22 , 26 , 27 ]. Of the five studies that did not find any evidence of differences, or found that White men had higher PSA levels than Black men, four of these studies were rated as poor quality [ 17 , 22 , 23 , 27 ]. Incidentally, three of these studies did not stratify by age [ 17 , 22 , 23 ] and the mean age of White men was greater than Black men in two of these [ 17 , 23 ]. All of the five studies that compared PSA levels of Hispanic men to White and Black men were assessed as good quality [ 18 , 19 , 21 , 24 , 26 ]. One of these studies found fewer Hispanic men experienced PSA values over 4 ng/mL compared to Black men, and while this was not an age-adjusted or age-stratified calculation, Hispanic men had a higher median age range than Black men [ 19 ]. The remaining four studies had a much smaller sample size of Hispanic men and found no evidence of differences in PSA values between Hispanic and Black men. None of the five studies reported a difference in PSA levels between Hispanic and White men; indeed, the summary values reported for these men appeared consistently similar across each study. Only two studies reported PSA levels for Asian men, and both found no difference between Asian men and men of other ethnic groups [ 18 , 28 ]. Finally, there was no evidence of differences in PSA levels between the Maori and Pacific Island ethnic groups in any of the three studies that reported PSA levels in New Zealand [ 28 – 30 ]. A difference was found in the age-adjusted mean difference between Maori and White men, with significantly higher PSA levels reported for White men [ 29 ]. However, in an almost identical cohort, this difference was not observed in Grey, et al. (2005) when assessing proportions of men with a PSA level above 4 ng/mL [ 30 ]. Discussion Key findings This systematic review found evidence that Black males had higher PSA levels than White males in the USA, with no published evidence from other countries with significant Black populations. Multiple studies suggested Hispanic men have similar PSA levels to White men in the USA, with one study reporting lower PSA levels in Hispanic men compared to Black men. In New Zealand, Maori men were found to have lower levels of PSA than White men and there were no differences between Maori men and Pacific Island men. There was no evidence of differences between the PSA levels of Asian men and men of other ethnic groups. Strengths and limitations The overarching strength of this study was the inclusion of 654 197 men. Importantly, studies were only selected if PSA values were collected for men within the same country to control for differences in healthcare systems and inter-country cultures, and age-stratified or age-adjusted PSA values were meticulously extracted where possible to control for the effects of age. A weakness was the availability of studies limited to the USA and New Zealand and a considerable underrepresentation of the Asian and Mixed ethnicities, major ethnic groups in many countries. A meta-analysis would have provided further certainty of differences in PSA values across the ethnic groups, although this was not possible due to the heterogeneity of reported PSA measures. Publication bias may have resulted in a higher number of publications reporting ethnic differences in PSA values. However, the outcome of four of the included studies was prostate cancer risk or urological outcomes [ 17 , 22 , 23 , 29 ], thus any reported ethnic differences in PSA values from the patient characteristics of these studies should have been free from publication bias. Indeed, Rhodes, et al . (2012b) [ 23 ] reported higher PSA levels in Black men compared to White men in their patient characteristics. Comparison to existing literature Ethnicity was found to be a source of significant heterogeneity in a recent systematic review assessing age-adjusted reference ranges in apparently healthy men: controlling for ethnicity in 10-year age intervals reduced study heterogeneity by 13% from 99% ( I 2 statistic) [ 16 ]. The remaining heterogeneity may have been explained, in part, by differences in inter-country cultures and healthcare systems, which was not controlled for. The study concluded ethnicity was an important parameter that influenced PSA levels and should be considered when clinically assessing PSA values. In a prostate cancer cohort in the UK including Black and White men, Black men were found to have higher PSA levels than White men at the point of diagnosis [ 31 ]. Despite this, Black men were diagnosed at similar clinical stages and had similar Gleason scores, and interestingly, preliminary data from the authors suggested there was no difference in prostate cancer mortality between Black and White men [ 32 ]. This starkly contrasts with abundant data from the USA reporting poorer prognosis in Black men [ 33 ] which may be attributed to the differences in healthcare systems between the two countries: access to healthcare in the USA varies significantly by income and deprivation, whereas healthcare in the UK is universally free at point of access. As deprivation levels are higher in Black men in the USA compared to White men, Black men may be less able or likely to access healthcare [ 34 ]. Asian men in the UK were reported to have lower incidence of prostate cancer than White men, with lower PSA levels at diagnosis and less aggressive disease at presentation [ 35 ]. Clinical implications The findings of this systematic review shed some light on PSA levels of men across different ethnic groups. Further research is needed to determine whether these differences are enough to warrant introducing ethnicity into guidance for interpreting PSA levels, and what the implications of that may be. The accuracy of PSA for the diagnosis of prostate cancer in different ethnic groups is unknown, as is whether higher PSA levels observed in Black men are due to higher prevalence of prostate cancer in that group, or whether higher PSA levels in Black men could be contributing to overdiagnosis. Any amendments to current guidance for interpreting PSA based on ethnicity will need to be carefully assessed with thorough modelling and evaluation taking into account prostate cancer incidence, stage at diagnosis and mortality to ensure it was reducing, rather than increasing, health inequalities in prostate cancer diagnosis. Conclusion Healthy Black men have higher PSA levels than White or Hispanic men, which reflects the higher rates of prostate cancer diagnosis in Black men. It is not known whether Black men are diagnosed with similar rates of clinically significant prostate cancer to White men, or whether raised PSA values are contributing to overdiagnosis in Black men. Future research needs to consider the impacts of PSA thresholds in Black men for triggering prostate cancer investigation, and whether ethnicity specific PSA thresholds could help to reduce the ethnic inequalities in prostate cancer diagnosis. documents.title: Exploring the potential clinical value of shear wave elastography in prostate cancer: a meta-analysis.
documents.abstract: The potential role of shear wave elastography (SWE) in prostate cancer (PCa) remains unclear. We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library databases to identify correlated studies up to Dec 2024. A total of 137 studies were identified for potential inclusion, and 11 studies were included, comprising 1551 PCa patients. The pooled sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for detecting malignant prostatic nodules were 90% (95% CI, 81-95%), 75% (95% CI, 62-84%) and 90% (95% CI: 87, 92%) in per-patient analysis, respectively. The sensitivity, specificity, and AUC were 86% (95% CI: 72%, 95%), 86% (95% CI: 78%, 92%) and 92% (95% CI: 90%, 94%) in per-sextant analysis. Publication bias test addressed low significant small-study bias. We found that SWE may serve as a potential diagnostic strategy for PCa and may help to reduce the number of core biopsies. Since limited quantity and small sample size of included studies, further well-designed studies are strongly encouraged to address this promising strategy.

Keywords Shear wave elastography Prostate cancer Diagnostic AUC Meta-analysis pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2025 Introduction Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common non-cutaneous malignancy in men of Western world. The consequences of misdiagnosing are the complications of radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy as well as the risk of delaying removal of the tumor [ 1 ]. Despite widely disparate attempts to ameliorate the risk of harboring PCa, randomized biopsies remain the gold standard for PCa diagnosis [ 2 ]. Logically, a rising prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level, or an abnormal digital rectal examination (DRE), triggers a transrectal ultrasound (TRUS)-guided 12-core biopsy [ 3 ]. Of note, the major drawback of biopsy is the high false negative rate in patients with indolent cancer [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, biopsies encompass the risk of acute bleeding, prostatitis or urinary retention. Nowadays the diagnosis of PCa is based principally on several imaging modalities, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), transrectal ultrasonography and elastography. MRI procedure requires an interdisciplinary modality and is more time-consuming than other imaging techniques [ 6 ]. While TRUS demonstrates high accuracy in the detection lesions, it hardly performs as well in differentiating malignant from benign foci. Elastography is a more sensitive and accurate method for estimating tissue stiffness and has exhibited good diagnostic performance in prostate cancer. However, this modality can only estimate tissue stiffness qualitatively and the force applied to create displacement is unstable [ 7 ]. To overcome these limitations, a technique called shear wave elastography (SWE) has recently been developed [ 8 ]. Recent synthesis confirmed the ability of SWE to detect cancer nodules with good accuracy and its superiority to grey scale ultrasound [ 9 ]. In contrast to elastography, SWE doesn’t require any compression on the rectal wall, therefore allows measurements of prostate tissue stiffness in quantitative values. Furthermore, SWE might result in a user-independent imaging of the PCa via calculation of elasticity ratios between benign and malignant prostate lesions [ 7 , 8 ]. To date, there was scarcity of evidence on the SWE diagnostic performance. Numerous studies have shown promising profile with SWE for the differential diagnosis of PCa, despite the discrepant finding from one aforementioned study [ 9 ]. Therefore, we systematically reviewed and conducted a meta-analysis of the currently available evidence to evaluate the performance of SWE in the diagnosis of PCa using the histopathologic specimen as the reference standard. Materials and methods Literature search strategy We carried out this systematic review according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis statement (PRISMA) [ 10 ] Guidelines. The databases including PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library and references of relevant articles were searched up to Dec 2024. The keywords used for search include:"Virtual Touch tissue quantification","acoustic radiation force impulse","shear wave elastography", and"prostate”. We combined these keywords with medical subject headings (MeSH) terms to ensure a comprehensive review. The detailed search strategies for PubMed database have been provided in supplemental material. There are no language restrictions and publication year limitation. This study has been registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD42024571276). Inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion criteria: 1) studies evaluating the diagnosis accuracy of SWE on the PCa detection; 2) studies using the histopathology evidence of the radical prostatectomy (RP) specimen as the referring standard, and 3) studies with available or derivable data to construct 2 × 2 contingency tables. All literature searches and assessments were conducted independently by two authors. Discrepancies were addressed via rechecking the searches and assessment process and any disagreements were consulted by a third author. Exclusion criteria: 1) studies containing less than 10 patients; and 2) studies with a maximum time interval for 3 months between SWE and RP. Study section and data extraction The data for calculating were extracted by means of a predefined form. Extracted baseline data included: first author, publication year, country or region, study design, number of participants, gold diagnostic standard, age(yr), prostate volume(ml), PSA level (ng/ml). Complete reported data (sensitivity, specificity) were necessary to calculate the true positive (TP), false positive (FP), false negative (FN) and true negative (TN) cases. If some studies did not provide data to directly construct 2 × 2 contingency tables, the diagnostic sensitivity and specificity provided in the articles were used to calculate related data and construct tables. Any disagreements in the process of study selection or data extraction were resolved by a third author. Quality assessment The quality of the trials was considered on the basis of Quality Assessment of Studies of Diagnostic Accuracy Included in Systematic Review 2 (QUADAS-2) [ 11 ]. This tool comprises four domains: index test, reference standard, patient selection and flow and timing. Each domain is evaluated concerning risk of bias, and the first three domains are also assessed regarding applicability. Statistical analysis This meta- analysis was based on the known values, including TP, TN, FP and FN data. The sensitivity and specificity of SWE were evaluated. The overall pooled sensitivity and specificity, positive likelihood ratio, negative likelihood ratio and diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) with corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI). Summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curves, area under the curve (AUC) and the Q* index were also computed [ 12 ]. Methods for diagnostic and screening tests were followed as well [ 13 , 14 ]. Between-study heterogeneity was evaluated through the use of computing Higgins I 2 [ 15 , 16 ]. An I 2 value > 20% or a p value < 0.05 was considered to indicate heterogeneity. All statistical analyses were performed using Meta-Disc Version 1.4 (Unit of Clinical Biostatistics, Ramon y Cajal Hospital, Madrid, Spain). Publication bias Begg’s test and funnel plot were also employed to estimate potential publication bias by STATA 12.0 (STATA, College Station, TX, USA) [ 17 ]. Result Literature search Our search initially identified 137 unique publications (Fig. 1 ). Of these, 46 were excluded subsequent to 57 full-text articles reviewed for eligibility. Studies were excluded on the grounds that they were inappropriate to the review question ( n = 20), lacking report on diagnostic result or provided insufficient data ( n = 23) and repetitive studies ( n = 3). Finally, 11 publications were included for meta-analysis, covering a total of 1551 patients. [ 18 – 28 ] Fig. 1 Flowchart of identification and selection of studies for the systematic review Study and patient characteristics Table 1 summarized the characteristics of the patients recruited in the studies. The median age in the studies ranged from 59 to 89 years, median PSA ranged from 6.7 to 8.5 ng/ml, median prostate volume ranged from 39 to 55 ml. 1551 patients were recruited consecutively in 11 studies [ 18 – 28 ]. The percentage of patients included with PCa varied from 28 to 100%. All 12 studies in which SWE examinations were carried out with an Aixplorer device from Supersonic Imagine. Overall, the quality of the research was moderate (Table 2 ). In terms of the patient selection domain, three studies [ 19 , 24 , 25 ] had a high risk of bias due to unclear inclusion or exclusion criteria. One study had a retrospective study design [ 21 ]. Four studies did not specify the threshold they used [ 18 , 21 , 23 , 25 ]. The description of the index test was not sufficient in three studies [ 18 , 22 , 23 ]. Blinding in interpreting the index test resultant effect against the reference-standard effect was revealed in five studies[ 19 , 20 , 24 , 25 , 28 ]. In terms of the reference standard domain, three studies [ 18 , 22 , 23 ] had a high risk of bias. Above all, the description of the reference test was sufficient in eight studies [ 19 – 21 , 24 – 28 ], but insufficient in the remaining studies. In light of the flow and timing domain, five studies had a high risk of bias, on the grounds that interval between histopathology and MRI was not specified [ 18 , 22 , 23 , 27 , 28 ], whereas in other studies, histopathology was obtained within three months following SWE. Studies with high bias risk (e.g., lack of blinding, n = 6) had slightly lower AUC (0.88 vs. 0.92 in low-bias studies), but the difference was not statistically significant ( p = 0.12). This suggests SWE’s accuracy is not heavily influenced by methodological flaws. Potential overestimation of specificity (86% vs. 75% in per-patient analysis) may exist, warranting larger, blinded studies. Diagnostic accuracy of SWE Results of meta-analysis to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy in studies are demonstrated in Table 3 . Data from five studies [ 20 , 22 , 24 , 26 , 28 ] that involved 1071 patients were used for per-patient synthesis. The sensitivity and specificity were 90% (95% CI, 81–95%) and 75% (95% CI, 62–84%) (Fig. 2 ), respectively. The area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 90% (95% CI, 87–92%) (Fig. 3 a). The estimate of Q* index was 14.45. The positive and negative likelihood ratio (LR) were 3.54 (95% CI, 2.29–5.49) and 0.13 (95% CI, 0.06–0.26), respectively. The summary diagnostic odds ratio was 27.23 (95% CI, 10.79–68.35). I 2 value was 83.04% (95% CI, 69.08%–97.01%) for sensitivity and 90.86% (95% CI, 84.47%–97.25%) for specificity. The sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic odds ratio were 86% (95% CI, 72%–95%), 86% (95% CI, 78%–92%), and 38.5 (95% CI, 10.87–136), respectively (Figs. 3 b and 4 ). Analysis was performed on per-patient ( a ) and per-sextant ( b ) basis. Considering a negative test, the post-test probability would be less than 3% and 4% respectively (Fig. 5 ). Fig. 5 Forest plots of studies included to compare estimated mean Young’s modulus (kPa) value between malignant and benign lesions with SWE. WMD = weighted mean difference Relationship of pathological outcomes with mean young’s modulus (kPa) value Four trials explored the correlation between prostate stiffness and pathological outcomes. Findings of meta-analysis manifested stiffness measured on the basis of Young’s modulus (kPa) value is a significant criterion for distinguishing between benign and malignant lesions, with a weighted mean difference of 28.62 kPa (95% CI, 16.43–40.82; P < 0.001) (Fig. 6 ). However, Porsch et al. [ 29 ] emphasized that the elasticity is not a considerable criterion for distinguishing between benign and malignant lesions with an area under the curve of 0.604 ± 0.023. Significantly higher for studies originating elsewhere compared with those originating from Asia in pooled sensitivity considering either patient or sextant analysis. Studies published previous to 2012 exhibits remarkable better specificity in both patient and sextant analysis. There was no remarkable difference in sensitivity or specificity for any of the assessed study characteristics. Among the quality factors considered, study QUADAS score, blinding and satisfactory description of index/reference test seemed to be associated with DOR. Out of these variables, solely the blinding was significant ( P = 0.01). None of the key baseline covariates demonstrated significant differences among the eleven studies encompassed in the per-patient or per-sextant diagnostic meta-analysis ( P > 0.05 for all). A low likelihood of publication bias for SWE on a per-patient basis ( P = 0.44) was observed from the linear regression test of funnel plot asymmetry. However, there was evidence of a high likelihood of publication bias on a per-lesion basis ( P = 0.03) (Supplemental Fig. 1 ). High heterogeneity (I 2 = 83–94%) likely stems from three factors: (1) Variability in SWE threshold definitions across studies (e.g., Young’s modulus cutoff ranges: 20–80 kPa); (2) Differences in biopsy protocols (systemic vs. fusion-guided); (3) Patient population variations (PSA levels: 6.7–8.5 ng/mL). Subgroup analysis showed Asian studies had lower sensitivity (85% vs. 92% in non-Asian cohorts), possibly due to smaller prostate volumes and operator training differences. Discussion PCa often requires aggressive therapy, such as surgical resection, radiotherapy, however a majority of benign nodules require peer follow-up. It has been reported that the sextant procedure misses 10% to 30% of cancers [ 30 ]. Thus, a precise diagnosis avoiding unnecessary surgeries and reducing medical costs is needed. SWE detected cancer nodules via ultrasound-based, real-time method. Specific differences in tissue elasticity are increasingly dispensed for detection and localisation of liver fibrosis as well as breast malignancies, and may also help reveal tumour lesions in the prostate [ 31 – 34 ]. When SWE is carried out, the tissue is mechanically excited to generate small tissue displacements. This result in shear wave propagation while being tracked to calculate the shear wave velocity (SWV) [ 35 , 36 ]. Furthermore, PCa foci was significantly stiffer than normal prostate tissue. Therefore, cancer foci can be identified in the prostate by SWE. Our meta-analysis indicated that quantitative SWE measurement is a non-invasive, reliable technique with considerable sensitivity and specificity in the detection of PCa nodules. It is valuable for the reason that clinical practice need modification due to the limitations of current modalities performed to diagnose PCa nodules. Based on preliminary profile [ 25 ], real-time quantitative SWE imaging has a potential clinical improvement in terms of clinical practice of PCa detection by allowing targeted biopsies of suspicious areas, thus attenuating both the cost and the complications associated with the current standard of care [ 37 ]. The test criteria of our result are comparable to that reported for MRI [ 38 ]. Delongchamps et al. [ 39 ] reported a sensitivity and specificity for cancer detection of 80% and 97% using MRI. In another study, MRI sensitivity was 89% to 91%, and specificity was 77% to 81% [ 40 ]. Interestingly, ultrasound characterization is a nonquantitative procedure which is invariably dependent on operator’s experience [ 41 ]. Elastography has had promising resultant effect in the diagnosis of prostate cancer, notwithstanding the major limitations of the intra- and inter-observer variabilities; Compared to it, SWE is much similar to a standard TRUS clinical examination as it does not require any additional compression [ 42 ]. Our analyses also presented disparate cutoff value for distinguishing suspected tissue for PCa can be employed by SWE. Such a cut-off ceased the inter-observer variability of SWE as a potential method for better imaging of PCa foci. Even inexperienced users can target tumor nodules to ameliorate the cancer detection rate [ 37 , 41 ]. In work evaluating learning curve of elastography [ 43 ], Heinzelbecker et al. reported an overall sensitivity and specificity in this learning cohort were 58% and 78%, respectively. Despite its tolerable and efficacy, SWE suffers from a major drawback: It limited penetration depth in the tissue to 3 to 4 cm. Enlarged prostate glands or multiple calcifications may limit the performance of SWE, especially for the detection of anterior tumors, based on these technical restricts [ 43 ]. The results of the compilation need to be concerned respecting the flaws of the primary studies recruited in the review and the review itself. As the QUADAS-2 ratings denoted, there are a number of details in the face of key methodological criteria were not reported. Blinding was found in some but not all studies. Lack of blind may artificially inflate the diagnostic performance. Meanwhile, there are also a number of caveats in interpreting our analysis. First, we carried out TRUS-guided and systemic biopsies as the gold standard for PC detection. Even though this procedure is the recommended diagnostic method in patients with the suspicion of PCa, there might be a risk of PCa underestimating [ 44 , 45 ]. This shortcoming could also explain the high false positive rate of SWE [ 43 ]. Second, though efforts were made to identify grey literature, there remains a likelihood of unpublished studies, thus we cannot rule out the possibility of publication bias. Further research is ongoing in this area and is expected to shed more light on this issue. Conclusions Our meta-analysis indicates that SWE could be a feasible technique instead of routine prostate examination in order to ameliorate PCa detection and biopsy success rate, especially in early prostate cancer, and we believe that it may reduce the unnecessary core biopsies required for diagnosis in the future. PCa elasticity values increase with Gleason score, thus seem linked to PCa aggressiveness especially. Large prospective multicenter studies are needed to confirm the results and further evaluate the potential of SWE in the detection of PCa. documents.title: Psychosocial experiences of prostate cancer survivors after treatment: a systematic review of qualitative studies.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prostate cancer, the second most common male malignancy worldwide, treatment-related complications cause both physical dysfunction and psychosocial sequelae, significantly impairing quality of life. Now requires integrated biopsychosocial rehabilitation beyond disease-focused treatment, comprehensive assessment of psychosocial adaptation and illness perception is essential for developing evidence-based, patient-centered rehabilitation strategies to optimize post-therapy recovery.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to systematically review and synthesize qualitative evidence on post-treatment psychosocial experiences in prostate cancer patients, thoroughly analyze patients' lived experiences and coping strategies, and provide an evidence-based foundation for establishing a tiered psychosocial support system and developing clinical intervention protocols.
METHODS: This systematic review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for qualitative meta-aggregation, with reporting structured according to the ENTREQ statement. Evidence was graded using the ConQual approach and critically appraised with the JBI Qualitative Assessment and Review Instrument (JBI-QARI). We systematically searched six major English databases for qualitative or mixed-methods studies investigating psychosocial experiences in post-treatment prostate cancer patients, with the literature search updated to February 28, 2024. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, followed by collaborative thematic synthesis to identify core themes.
RESULTS: A total of 22 studies from 12 countries were included, with 65 findings extracted and categorized into 4 synthesized findings consisting of 8 distinct categories: (1) Psychological and emotional responses (fear and anxiety responses, depression and emotional distress); (2) Healthcare information and systemic barriers (disease-related information needs, barriers in healthcare systems); (3) Social support and interpersonal adaptation (support system needs, social role and relationship adaptation); (4) Internal adaptation and external actions (internal psychological adjustment, external coping behaviors).
CONCLUSION: Prostate cancer survivors face multifaceted psychosocial challenges during post-treatment recovery, with psychological and social responses impacting rehabilitation outcomes. Inadequate social support systems and gaps in healthcare information emerge as major barriers to recovery. To address these issues, healthcare providers should enhance communication effectiveness, while policymakers need to strengthen social support networks, government and corporate sectors should implement targeted policies, and family members should provide empathetic understanding and active encouragement, collectively fostering comprehensive patient support.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/recorddashboard, CRD42024537363.
